list.listitem: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a clinical diagnosis based on four diagnostic criteria: (1) urge to move legs, usually associated with uncomfortable or unpleasant sensations; (2) symptoms begin or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity; (3) symptoms partially or totally relieved by movement; (4) symptoms worse or occur only in the evening or night. C
RLS may be primary or secondary to iron deficiency, pregnancy, renal failure, or medications. C
Consider checking serum ferritin and a basic metabolic panel to rule out secondary causes. C

Independent of ferritin level or route of administration, oral or intravenous iron supplementation may improve symptoms of RLS compared to placebo and may be comparable to pramipexole, but it has uncertain effects on quality of life. B
American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines (2025) recommend against the routine long-term use of pramipexole, rotigotine, and ropinorole, favoring instead gabapentin and pregabalin.B
Exercise should be encouraged as it may improve symptoms. B

background.definition: RLS is a neurologic movement disorder characterized by an irresistible urge to move the legs, occurring during times of inactivity and often interfering with sleep.

list.listitem: RLS affects 1.5% to 15% of the adult population, depending on the definition. Prevalence increases with advancing age. Approximately 30% of those with RLS have symptoms severe enough to consider medical treatment.
Consequences of sleep disturbance common in individuals with RLS.
Overall quality of life lower for individuals with RLS.
Depression and anxiety commonly associated with RLS.
Primary RLS has a familial component and is more common in females and with advancing age.
RLS may be secondary to iron deficiency (with or without anemia), chronic kidney disease, pregnancy, or medications.
RLS is also associated with some medications, including atypical antipsychotic drugs.
An association with ankylosing spondylitis has been described (31% vs 13% in healthy controls in a case control study with 91 patients).
The prevalence of RLS in patients with migraine was reported to be 16% in a meta-analysis.
An association with other movement disorders is unclear.
Pathophysiology of RLS is not fully understood.
Abnormal CNS dopamine activity and iron function are found in individuals with RLS.
Include a general sleep question in the review of systems, such as "Have you been sleeping well recently?" C
Diagnosis is based on history and exclusion of conditions such as neuropathy, anemia, and vascular disease (see ). C
Consider checking serum ferritin and a basic metabolic panel to rule out secondary causes; extensive diagnostic testing is not usually indicated. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Palpable muscle tightening with sudden onset.
Not associated with inactivity or helped by movement and no exacerbation with evenings or night.
Usually associated with neuroleptic medications, causing internal desire to move, not associated with limb discomfort, and no evening exacerbation.

list.listitem: Patients may complain of trouble sleeping.
Uncomfortable sensations are often hard to describe, and words/phrases such as "aching," "crawling," "worms under my skin," or "I have to move" may be used.

Diagnosis based on four criteria: (1) urge to move the legs, usually associated with uncomfortable or unpleasant sensations in the legs; (2) symptoms begin or worsen during periods of rest or inactivity such as lying or sitting; (3) symptoms partially or totally relieved by movement; (4) symptoms worse or occur only in the evening or night.
Supporting criteria include: (1) periodic limb movements of sleep; (2) family history of RLS; (3) response to dopaminergic therapy.
Obtain a history of vascular disease, diabetes, neuropathy to rule out other causes of leg pains and a medication history to rule out secondary causes of RLS.
Perform a focused physical examination to rule out neuropathy, vascular disease.

American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines (2024) recommend obtaining serum ferritin and transferrin saturation to rule out iron deficiency. This should be measured in the morning at least 24 hours after the last dose of iron supplements.
Obtain basic metabolic panel to rule out uremia or diabetes.
Polysomnography, imaging studies, and nerve conduction studies are generally not necessary.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines (2025) recommend against the routine long-term use of pramipexole, rotigotine and ropinirole, favoring instead gabapentin and pregabalin.B

Independent of ferritin level or route of administration, oral or intravenous iron supplementation may improve symptoms of restless leg syndrome (RLS) compared to placebo and may be comparable to pramipexole, but it has uncertain effects on quality of life. B
Opioids may help reduce pain and improve sleep quality in the short-term, but long-term safety is uncertain. B

American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines (2025) recommend gabapentin or pregabalin for treatment of RLS. Based on low certainty evidence they also favor dipyridamole and extended release oxycodone. AASM guidelines recommend against routine long-term use of ramipexole, transdermal rotigotine, and ropinirole (although short-term use is acceptable). The AASM guidelines also recommend against use of bupropion, carbamazepine, clonazepam, valerian, valproic acid, and cabergoline. While
All patients with iron deficiency should be treated with oral or IV iron supplementation. The threshold for treatment is a serum ferritin < 75 ng/ml for adults and < 50 ng/ml for children.

Nonergotamine dopamine agonists ropinirole, rotigotine (transdermal) and pramipexole are effective in the treatment of moderate to severe RLS (defined as symptoms occurring at least 15 days per month or severe enough to effect negatively the quality of life). Systematic reviews found improvements in sleep parameters and disease specific quality of life.

However, nonergot dopamine agonists such as ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine, and sumanirole are effective for RLS but have side effects such as nausea, sedation, and fatigue. Therefore, AASM guidelines (2024) recommend against routine use of pramipexole, transdermal rotigotine, and ropinirole.
A systematic review of rotigotine (Neupro), a transdermal a patch, identified 6 RCTs. There was improvement compared with placebo based on the International Restless Leg Scale.

Ergot-derived dopamine agonists cabergoline and pergolide are effective. However, they carry a small risk of cardiac valvulopathy, especially at doses above 3 mg/day and if taken for more than 6 months. The absolute risk is about 2.5 additional cases of valve damage for every 1000 patients who take these drugs for more than a year.

Levodopa/carbidopa improves symptoms in the short term, but augmentation is a significant problem, limiting usefulness in individuals requiring daily medications. Augmentation refers to symptoms occurring earlier in the day and more widespread (ie, including arms). Augmentation may also occur with dopamine agonists but is probably less common than with levodopa.
AASM guidelines recommend against use of levodopa for this reason.

Opioids may improve symptoms, but have significant risks and adverse effects, especially in older patients, such as an increased risk of falls. A Cochrane review of a single RCT with a high drop-out rate noted that opioids may be effective in the treatment of RLS symptoms but its safety is uncertain, especially long-term.
A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating the efficacy of benzodiazepines for patients with RLS.
If the patient requires an antidepressant, bupropion is least likely antidepressant to exacerbate symptoms.
Studies in uremic patients with RLS are lacking, but levodopa, dopaminergic agonists, and seizure medications may be effective.
A randomized crossover trial with 24 patients found a significant benefit of botulinum toxin injections in patients with moderate to severe RLS.
A systematic review only identified a single RCT of magnesium for RLS, which found no benefit.

A Cochrane review identified 10 studies with 428 participants. Based on low quality evidence, iron supplementation may improve restlessness but there is little evidence to suggest improvement in other outcomes. Patients with iron deficiency anemia should, of course, be appropriately treated. Based on prespecified subgroup analyses, level of ferritin and route of administration (ie, oral vs intravenous) do not appear to affect efficacy of iron supplementation. Finally, iron supplementation appears to have similar efficacy compared to pramipexole.
A Cochrane review identified 2 poor quality studies with 170 patients of acupuncture. One found no benefit, the other mixed evidence of benefit.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines (2024) recommend addressing alcohol and caffeine use, serotonergic and antidopaminergic medications, and untreated sleep apnea.
Exercise consisting of aerobics and lower body resistance training may be effective.

Tonic motor activation (TOMAC) uses a wearable device that stimulates peroneal nerves. It triggers a sustained activation of the tibialis anterior muscle, engaging neuromuscular circuits without causing movement. A systematic review of 4 RCTs with 320 patients found that TOMAC significantly reduced symptom scores and was well tolerated.
Among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) with RLS, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of exercise programs during dialysis and for pharmacologic treatments.
A network meta-analysis of 24 RCTs with 1252 participants on dialysis that using a cool dialysate reduced severity the most. Gabapentin was also effective.
Consider discontinuing medications that may exacerbate RLS, most notably antihistamines, SSRIs, caffeine, and neuroleptics.
Consider a trial of abstinence from caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol.
A small study (n = 35) found benefit with use of pneumatic compression devices.
A small randomized trial (n=52) in pregnant women with RLS found that progressive muscle relaxation exercises reduced RLS intensity and improved quality of life and sleep.
Treatment of the underlying condition may improve or resolve symptoms of RLS. C
RLS is more common in women and progresses with advancing age. C
Seek medical advice for sleep disturbance or reduced quality of life caused by unusual sensation in legs, relieved only by movement.
Treatment recommendations are similar for the elderly.
Dopamine agonists should be used with caution and at lowest effective dose because of the risk of orthostasis (other side effects include nausea and daytime somnolence).

RLS occurs commonly in pregnancy, usually during the third trimester (affects as many as 25% of patients). No medications are recommended during pregnancy, and symptoms will likely improve or resolve following pregnancy.
Up to one-third of individuals with RLS report symptoms before age 18 years.
Criteria for the diagnosis of RLS in children are similar to those for adults.

The child should describe in his or her own words symptoms consistent with leg discomfort, OR two of the following three supportive criteria should be present: (1) sleep disturbance, (2) biologic parent or sibling with definite RLS, (3) polysomnographic documentation of periodic limb movement index of 5 or more per hour of sleep.
Focus on good sleep hygiene, exercise, and caffeine restriction.
No recommendations can be made regarding the use of dopaminergic medications in children.

cell.label: Meet all four diagnostic criteria for RLS (urge to move legs associated with unpleasant sensation, symptoms begin or worsen with rest or inactivity, symptoms relieved by movement, and worse or only occurring at night)?
Patient pregnant or on medications which may cause RLS?
Order ferritin and basic metabolic panel to rule out secondary causes.
Primary RLS. Recommend exercise, discontinue possibly offending medications, and consider dopamine agonist.
Likely secondary RLS. Treat underlying condition. Improves RLS?
